summary: Psalm 107 opens Book V by calling the redeemed and gathered people to give thanks to Yahweh. It then gives four scenes of distress and rescue: wanderers without a city, prisoners in darkness, the sick near death, and sailors in a storm. The final section widens the view to reversals in land, rulers, the needy, the upright, and the wicked, ending with a call to pay attention to Yahweh’s loving kindnesses.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers many kinds of danger into one repeated pattern: trouble, crying out, deliverance, and public praise. As the first psalm of Book V, it turns the collection toward return, thanksgiving, and wisdom after the darker questions of earlier books.

context.author: Psalms is a many-writer anthology; Psalm 107 does not name an individual author in the chapter text.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also using the Psalms for prayer and praise.
context.date: The Psalms preserve material from different periods, and the final five-book collection is later than many individual poems; a single date for Psalm 107 is not established by the chapter.
context.setting: Book V of the Psalter, where thanksgiving, return, Torah, pilgrimage, and praise become prominent. The chapter imagines people gathered from many lands and uses wilderness, prison, illness, sea, farmland, and public assembly as its scenes.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic thanksgiving with repeated refrains, vivid rescue scenes, and a closing wisdom appeal.

outline.heading: Call for the redeemed to speak
outline.note: The psalm begins with thanks because Yahweh is good, then summons those redeemed and gathered from every direction to say so.

outline.heading: Wanderers led to a city
outline.note: People lost in a desert cry out in hunger and thirst; Yahweh delivers, leads them by a straight way, and satisfies the hungry soul.

outline.heading: Prisoners brought out of darkness
outline.note: Those bound in darkness because they rejected God’s words cry out, and Yahweh breaks their chains and the barriers that held them.

outline.heading: The sick healed near death
outline.note: Fools afflicted because of disobedience come near the gates of death; Yahweh sends his word, heals them, and the psalm calls for thanksgiving and song.

outline.heading: Sailors rescued from the storm
outline.note: Seafarers see Yahweh’s wonders in the deep, reach their wits’ end in a storm, cry out, and are brought to a calm haven; the assembly is told to praise him.

outline.heading: Reversals in land and society
outline.note: Yahweh turns water into desert and desert into water, settles the hungry and gives harvests, humbles princes, lifts the needy, and calls the wise to consider his loving kindnesses.

keyVerses.text: Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.
keyVerses.why: This opening line names the reason for the whole psalm’s thanksgiving.

keyVerses.text: Then they cried to Yahweh in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses.
keyVerses.why: This begins the repeated rescue pattern that structures the first distress scene and echoes through the chapter.

keyVerses.text: He makes the storm a calm, so that its waves are still.
keyVerses.why: The sea scene gives one of the chapter’s clearest pictures of danger changed into peace.

keyVerses.text: Whoever is wise will pay attention to these things. They will consider the loving kindnesses of Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: The final verse tells readers how to respond: not only with emotion, but with attentive reflection.

questions.question: Who are “the redeemed by Yahweh”?
questions.answer: In this chapter they are the people Yahweh has rescued from the hand of the adversary and gathered from many lands. The psalm does not pause to identify one historical event with certainty, though its language naturally fits a community remembering rescue and return.

questions.question: Why does the same pattern repeat several times?
questions.answer: The repetition teaches the reader to recognize a pattern across different kinds of distress. Wanderers, prisoners, the sick, and sailors all reach trouble, cry to Yahweh, receive deliverance, and are called to praise. The repeated refrain makes individual rescues part of a shared testimony.

questions.question: What does “loving kindness” mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase appears at the beginning, in the repeated praise calls, and at the end. In this chapter it points to Yahweh’s enduring goodness shown through rescue, provision, healing, and reversal. The psalm’s focus is not an abstract definition but a series of examples.

questions.question: Are the four distress scenes meant to be literal events, symbols, or both?
questions.answer: The chapter presents them as concrete scenes: a desert way, darkness and iron, sickness near death, and ships in great waters. Readers differ on whether the psalm is naming separate testimonies, poetic examples of many kinds of rescue, or images gathered around Israel’s larger experience of being restored. The text itself emphasizes the common pattern more than a single backstory.

questions.question: Does the psalm say every suffering person caused their own suffering?
questions.answer: No. Some scenes explicitly connect distress with rebellion, disobedience, or wickedness, especially the prisoners and the fools. But the wanderers and sailors are not blamed in the same way. The chapter is describing several forms of trouble, not giving one rule for all suffering.

questions.question: Why are the sailors included in a psalm about Yahweh’s rescue?
questions.answer: The sailors see Yahweh’s deeds and wonders in the deep, where the storm lifts them up and drops them down until they are at their wits’ end. Their rescue shows that Yahweh’s help is not limited to land, city, or temple space. The scene also turns a terrifying natural setting into another place for thanksgiving.

questions.question: What are “the sacrifices of thanksgiving”?
questions.answer: The phrase names an offered response after rescue. In this chapter, the sacrifice is paired with declaring Yahweh’s deeds with singing, so gratitude is both ritual and public testimony. The psalm does not give procedural details here; it emphasizes thankful acknowledgment.

questions.question: Why does the last section talk about rivers, deserts, rulers, and the needy?
questions.answer: After the four rescue scenes, the psalm broadens into examples of reversal. Yahweh can dry up fruitful places because of wickedness, water a desert, settle the hungry, humble rulers, and lift the needy. The point is that the same loving kindness seen in individual rescues can also be considered in the changing fortunes of land and society.

questions.question: What does the final verse ask readers to do?
questions.answer: It asks the wise person to pay attention and consider. The chapter does not leave its stories as background noise; it tells readers to notice what the repeated rescues and reversals reveal about Yahweh’s loving kindnesses.

glossary.def: Rescued or bought back from another power; in this chapter, those redeemed by Yahweh are gathered from many lands and called to speak.
An enemy or opposing power from whose hand Yahweh has rescued the redeemed.
A desolate, unsettled place where the wanderers find no city to live in and grow hungry and thirsty.
An image for extreme darkness and danger, used of those bound in affliction and later rescued.
Offerings of gratitude named alongside declaring Yahweh’s deeds with singing.
The safe harbor or destination reached after Yahweh calms the storm.
